title: Git Basics
description: The everyday Git commands — init, clone, add, commit, status, log, diff — and how to write good commit messages.
content:
These are the commands you'll type dozens of times a day. Get comfortable with them before moving on to branching.

## Starting a repository

`git init` creates a `.git` folder in the current directory — that folder *is* the repository. `git clone` does the same thing, but also downloads all history from a remote and points it at that remote automatically (see [Working with Remotes](/docs/git-workflow/remotes)).

## Checking status

```bash showLineNumbers
git status
```

Run this constantly. It tells you which files are untracked, modified, or staged — i.e., exactly where you are in the [three-area model](/docs/git-workflow/introduction#gits-three-area-mental-model).

## Staging changes

```bash showLineNumbers
git add file.go          # stage one file
git add file1.go file2.go # stage multiple files
git add .                 # stage everything in the current directory
git add -p                # interactively stage parts of a file (hunks)
```

## Committing

```bash showLineNumbers
git commit -m "Add rate limiting to auth endpoint"
```

A commit is a permanent snapshot of the staged changes, with a message explaining *why*. Useful flags:

```bash showLineNumbers
git commit -am "message"   # stage all tracked, modified files AND commit (skips new/untracked files)
git commit --amend         # rewrite the most recent commit (message and/or staged changes)
```

### Writing good commit messages

A widely used convention is **Conventional Commits**: `<type>: <short summary>`.

```bash showLineNumbers
git commit -m "feat: add JWT refresh token endpoint"
git commit -m "fix: prevent nil pointer on empty request body"
git commit -m "docs: update README with setup instructions"
git commit -m "refactor: extract validation logic into helper"
git commit -m "test: add table-driven tests for parser"
git commit -m "chore: bump go.mod dependencies"
```

Common types: `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `refactor`, `test`, `chore`, `perf`. This convention is what makes tools like automated changelogs and semantic-version bumping possible — and it's simply easier for a human to scan `git log` when every message starts with intent.

## Viewing history

```bash showLineNumbers
git log                    # full history
git log --oneline          # one line per commit
git log --oneline --graph  # with branch/merge visualization
git log -p                 # show the actual diff for each commit
git log --author="Alice"   # filter by author
```

## Viewing changes (diff)

```bash showLineNumbers
git diff              # unstaged changes vs last commit
git diff --staged     # staged changes vs last commit
git diff HEAD~1 HEAD   # changes between two commits
```

## Best practices

* **Commit often, in small units.** A commit should represent one logical change — easy to review, easy to revert if it's wrong.
* **Write the "why," not the "what."** The diff already shows *what* changed; the message should explain *why* (context a diff can't capture).
* **Never commit secrets.** `.env` files, API keys, credentials — see [.gitignore & Git Hooks](/docs/git-workflow/gitignore-hooks) for how to prevent this before it happens.
* **Run `git status` before `git add`,** and `git diff --staged` before `git commit` — know exactly what you're about to commit.

title: Best Practices Cheatsheet
description: A condensed, one-page reference of everything in the Git Workflow section.
content:
The full reasoning behind each of these lives on the earlier pages — this page is just the condensed reference to skim when you already know the concepts and need a quick reminder.

## Commits

* Commit small, logical, single-purpose changes — not "end of day" dumps.
* Use [Conventional Commits](/docs/git-workflow/basics#writing-good-commit-messages): `feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`, `refactor:`, `test:`, `chore:`.
* Write the *why*, not the *what* — the diff already shows what changed.
* Never commit secrets. Use `.gitignore` + environment variables (see [.gitignore & Git Hooks](/docs/git-workflow/gitignore-hooks)).
* `git diff --staged` before every `git commit` — know exactly what you're about to commit.
* Never `--amend` or rewrite a commit that's already been pushed and shared.

## Branching

* Name branches by intent: `feature/x`, `fix/x`, `chore/x` — never `test`, `wip`, `asdf`.
* Keep branches short-lived. Merge or rebase from `main` frequently to avoid painful conflicts later.
* Delete branches after merging — both locally (`git branch -d`) and on the remote.
* Default to [Feature Branch Workflow](/docs/git-workflow/workflow-strategies) unless you have a specific reason for Git Flow or Trunk-Based.

## Rebase vs Merge

* `rebase` only on branches that are **local and unshared**. Never rebase a branch others have pulled.
* `merge` is always safe, including on shared branches — it never rewrites history.
* Use `rebase -i` to clean up your own commits (squash, reword) before opening a PR.

## Remotes

* `git fetch` first if unsure what's changed remotely — it's always safe and non-destructive.
* Pull (or rebase) before you push; push is rejected if the remote has moved ahead of you.
* Never `--force` push to `main` or any shared branch. Prefer `--force-with-lease` on your own branches.

## Undoing changes

| Situation | Command |
|---|---|
| Discard uncommitted file changes | `git restore <file>` |
| Unstage a file | `git restore --staged <file>` |
| Shelve work temporarily | `git stash` |
| Undo a local, unpushed commit | `git reset --soft/--hard HEAD~1` |
| Undo a pushed/shared commit | `git revert <commit>` |

## Conflicts

1. `git status` to see conflicted files.
2. Open each file, resolve manually, delete all `<<<<<<<` / `=======` / `>>>>>>>` markers.
3. `git add <file>` for each resolved file.
4. `git commit` (merge) or `git rebase --continue` (rebase).
5. **Run your tests** before considering it done — a conflict with no markers left can still be logically wrong.
6. `git merge --abort` / `git rebase --abort` to bail out cleanly at any point.

## Pull request etiquette

* Keep PRs small and focused — easier and faster to review, easier to revert if something's wrong.
* Write a description that explains *why*, links related issues/tickets, and calls out anything reviewers should pay special attention to.
* Respond to review comments with either a fix or a clear counter-argument — don't silently ignore feedback.
* Make sure CI (tests, lint) passes before requesting review.
* Squash noisy "fix typo" / "address review" commits before merge (via `rebase -i` or the platform's "Squash and merge" button).

title: Branching & Merging
description: Isolating work in branches, and bringing it back into main with git merge.
content:
## Why branch?

A branch is just a movable pointer to a commit. Branching lets you work on a feature or fix in isolation, without touching the stable code on `main`, and without your half-finished work affecting teammates.

## Creating and switching branches

```bash showLineNumbers
git branch feature/rate-limiting     # create a branch (doesn't switch to it)
git switch feature/rate-limiting     # switch to it
# or, in one step:
git switch -c feature/rate-limiting  # create AND switch

git branch                           # list local branches
git branch -a                        # list local + remote branches
```

## The branching model

```bash showLineNumbers
git switch -c feature/rate-limiting
# ... make changes, commit ...
git add .
git commit -m "feat: add token bucket rate limiter"
```

Your branch diverges from `main` at the point you created it. You commit freely on your branch while `main` may keep moving (other people merging their own work) — Git tracks both histories independently until you merge.

## Merging

Once your feature branch is ready, merge it back into `main`:

```bash showLineNumbers
git switch main
git pull                       # make sure main is up to date first
git merge feature/rate-limiting
```

Two possible outcomes:

* **Fast-forward merge** — if `main` hasn't moved since you branched, Git just moves the `main` pointer forward. No merge commit is created.
* **Three-way merge** — if `main` *has* moved (someone else merged first), Git creates a new **merge commit** with two parents, combining both histories.

```bash showLineNumbers
git merge --no-ff feature/rate-limiting   # force a merge commit even if fast-forward is possible
```

## Deleting a branch after merge

```bash showLineNumbers
git branch -d feature/rate-limiting     # safe delete (refuses if not merged)
git branch -D feature/rate-limiting     # force delete (even if not merged)
git push origin --delete feature/rate-limiting  # delete on the remote too
```

## Best practices

* **Branch names should say what they do:** `feature/rate-limiting`, `fix/nil-pointer-auth`, `chore/upgrade-deps` — not `test`, `new-branch`, `asdf`.
* **Keep branches short-lived.** The longer a branch lives without merging, the more it diverges from `main` and the more painful the eventual merge/conflict resolution becomes.
* **Pull `main` before you branch, and again before you merge**, so you're working from the latest code.
* **Delete branches after merging.** A repo with 200 stale branches is a repo nobody trusts.

title: .gitignore & Git Hooks
description: Keeping build artifacts and secrets out of your repository, and automating checks before commits with Git hooks.
content:
## `.gitignore`

A `.gitignore` file tells Git which files/patterns to never track — build output, dependencies, local secrets, IDE settings. It lives at the repo root (nested `.gitignore` files are also allowed for folder-specific rules).

```bash showLineNumbers title=".gitignore (Go project example)"
# Binaries
/bin/
*.exe
*.test

# Dependency directories
/vendor/

# Environment / secrets
.env
.env.local
*.pem

# IDE
.vscode/
.idea/

# OS
.DS_Store
```

### Checking what's ignored

```bash showLineNumbers
git check-ignore -v path/to/file   # confirms which rule is ignoring a file (useful for debugging)
git status --ignored                # lists ignored files too
```

## Git Hooks

Hooks are scripts Git runs automatically at points in the workflow (before a commit, before a push, after a merge, etc.). They live in `.git/hooks/` as plain shell scripts, but that folder isn't committed to the repo by default — which is why most teams use a tool to manage and share hooks.

### A raw hook example

```bash showLineNumbers title=".git/hooks/pre-commit"
#!/bin/sh
# Run tests before allowing a commit
go test ./... || {
  echo "Tests failed — commit aborted."
  exit 1
}
```

Make it executable: `chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit`. Now `git commit` will run this first, and abort the commit if tests fail.

### Common hook points

| Hook | Runs when | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `pre-commit` | Before a commit is created | Lint, format, run fast tests |
| `commit-msg` | After the commit message is written | Enforce message format (e.g. Conventional Commits) |
| `pre-push` | Before `git push` | Run the full test suite, block push on failure |
| `post-merge` | After a merge completes | Auto-install dependencies if `go.mod` changed |

### Sharing hooks across a team

Because `.git/hooks/` isn't committed, teams typically use a tool like **[Husky](https://typicode.github.io/husky/)** (Node projects) or **[pre-commit](https://pre-commit.com/)** (language-agnostic, popular in Go/Python projects) to define hooks in a versioned config file and install them automatically for every contributor.

```bash showLineNumbers title="pre-commit example (.pre-commit-config.yaml)"
repos:
  - repo: local
    hooks:
      - id: go-fmt
        name: gofmt
        entry: gofmt -l -w
        language: system
        types: [go]
      - id: go-vet
        name: go vet
```

title: Introduction to Version Control
description: Why version control exists, and Git's core mental model — working directory, staging area, and repository.
content:
## What is version control?

Version control is a system that records changes to files over time, so you can recall specific versions later. Without it, "backup" usually means files named `final.go`, `final_v2.go`, `final_v2_ACTUALLY_FINAL.go` — which breaks down the moment more than one person touches the code.

A version control system (VCS) gives you:

* **History** — every change, who made it, and why (via commit messages).
* **Branching** — the ability to work on a new feature or fix without touching working code.
* **Collaboration** — multiple people editing the same codebase without overwriting each other.
* **Safety** — the ability to undo a bad change and recover previous states.

**Git** is a *distributed* VCS: every developer has a full copy of the repository's history on their own machine, not just a snapshot from a central server. This is why most Git operations (commit, log, diff, branch) work instantly and offline — only `push`/`pull`/`fetch` need the network.

## Git's three-area mental model

Understanding Git means understanding three areas a file passes through:

1. **Working Directory** — the actual files on disk that you edit.
2. **Staging Area (Index)** — a draft of your next commit. You choose exactly which changes go in.
3. **Repository (`.git` directory)** — the permanent, committed history.

This staging step is what makes Git different from simpler VCS tools: you don't commit "everything that changed," you commit *exactly what you `git add`ed* — which is what enables small, focused, atomic commits (more on that in [Git Basics](/docs/git-workflow/basics)).

## A file's lifecycle

Every file in a Git repository is in one of these states:

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Untracked** | Git doesn't know about this file yet (new file, never `git add`ed). |
| **Unmodified / Tracked** | Committed, and unchanged since the last commit. |
| **Modified** | Tracked, and changed since the last commit — but not staged. |
| **Staged** | Modified, and marked (via `git add`) to go into the next commit. |

`git status` (covered next) tells you exactly which state every file is in — it's the single most-used command in this entire guide.

## Why this matters for you

As a first-jobber, most of the pain with Git doesn't come from not knowing commands — it comes from not knowing *which area* a change currently lives in. "I committed but my teammate doesn't see it" (it's in your local repo, not pushed). "I `git add`ed but it's not in my commit" (you edited the file again after staging it — the working directory changed again). Keeping this three-area model in your head resolves 90% of Git confusion before it starts.

title: Rebase vs Merge
description: Two different ways to combine branch histories, the trade-offs, and when to use each.
content:
Both `merge` and `rebase` integrate changes from one branch into another — but they produce very different history shapes.

## Merge: preserves history exactly as it happened

```bash showLineNumbers
git switch main
git merge feature/rate-limiting
```

Merge creates a new **merge commit** joining both branch tips. The original commits on both branches stay exactly as they were. Nothing is rewritten — which makes merge always safe, even on shared/public branches.

## Rebase: replays your commits on top of another branch

```bash showLineNumbers
git switch feature/rate-limiting
git rebase main
```

Rebase takes your branch's commits, temporarily removes them, replays `main`'s new commits, then re-applies yours **one by one on top** — as if you'd branched off the latest `main` all along. The result is a straight, linear history with no merge commit. Note the commits get **new hashes** (`D'`, `E'`) — this is a history rewrite.

## The golden rule of rebase

## Interactive rebase

`git rebase -i` lets you edit, reorder, squash, or drop commits before they land — commonly used to clean up a messy feature branch before opening a pull request.

```bash showLineNumbers
git rebase -i HEAD~3
```

This opens an editor listing your last 3 commits:

```text showLineNumbers
pick a1b2c3d feat: add rate limiter skeleton
pick e4f5g6h fix typo
pick i7j8k9l feat: add tests

# Commands:
# p, pick   = use commit as-is
# r, reword = use commit, edit the message
# s, squash = combine with previous commit, keep both messages
# f, fixup  = combine with previous commit, discard this message
# d, drop   = remove commit entirely
```

Changing `pick` to `squash`/`fixup` on the "fix typo" line folds that noisy commit into the previous one, so your PR shows 2 clean commits instead of 3 messy ones.

## Which one should you use?

| Situation | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Updating your local feature branch with the latest `main` | `rebase` (keeps history linear, easier to review) |
| Merging a finished feature branch into `main` via PR | `merge` (most teams; GitHub/GitLab "Squash and merge" is a common middle ground) |
| The branch is shared with teammates | `merge` only — never rebase it |
| Cleaning up your own messy commits before opening a PR | `rebase -i` |

title: Working with Remotes
description: Connecting to a remote repository — remote, fetch, pull, push, and tracking branches.
content:
## What is a remote?

A remote is a pointer to another copy of the repository — usually hosted on GitHub, GitLab, or similar. By convention, the remote you cloned from is named `origin`.

```bash showLineNumbers
git remote -v                                  # list remotes and their URLs
git remote add origin https://github.com/org/repo.git   # add a remote (if you started with git init)
```

## fetch vs pull

This distinction trips up a lot of beginners:

```bash showLineNumbers
git fetch origin    # download new commits/branches from the remote, but do NOT merge them
git pull origin main # fetch AND merge (or rebase, if configured) into your current branch
```

`git fetch` is always safe — it just updates your local knowledge of the remote (`origin/main`) without touching your working files. `git pull` immediately integrates those changes into your current branch, which can trigger a merge or a conflict right away.

## Pushing your work

```bash showLineNumbers
git push origin feature/rate-limiting          # push a branch for the first time
git push -u origin feature/rate-limiting        # same, but also set upstream tracking
git push                                        # once tracking is set, just this works
```

The `-u` (`--set-upstream`) flag links your local branch to a remote branch, so future `git push`/`git pull` on that branch don't need the full `origin <branch>` every time — and `git status` will tell you if you're ahead/behind the remote.

## Tracking branches

```bash showLineNumbers
git status                 # shows "Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by 2 commits"
git branch -vv              # shows every local branch and what it tracks
```

## Force pushing

```bash showLineNumbers
git push --force              # dangerous: overwrites remote history
git push --force-with-lease   # safer: fails if the remote has commits you haven't seen
```

## Best practices

* **Pull before you push.** If the remote has moved, push will simply be rejected — fetch/pull (or rebase) first.
* **Push early, push often** on your own feature branches — it's a free backup and lets teammates see your work-in-progress.
* **Never force-push to `main` or any shared branch.**
* **Set up a tracking branch (`-u`)** the first time you push a new branch, so subsequent commands are simpler.

title: Resolving Merge Conflicts
description: A calm, step-by-step approach to resolving Git merge conflicts.
content:
A conflict happens when Git can't automatically decide how to combine two changes — usually because both branches edited the **same lines** of the **same file**. It is not an error and not a sign you did something wrong; it's expected in collaborative work.

## What a conflict looks like

When `git merge` or `git pull` hits a conflict, it pauses and marks the affected file(s):

```text showLineNumbers
func RateLimit(r *http.Request) bool {
<<<<<<< HEAD
    return tokenBucket.Allow(r.RemoteAddr)
=======
    return slidingWindow.Allow(r.RemoteAddr)
>>>>>>> feature/rate-limiting
}
```

* `<<<<<<< HEAD` down to `=======` — the version on **your current branch**.
* `=======` down to `>>>>>>> feature/rate-limiting` — the version from **the branch being merged in**.

## Step-by-step resolution

## Backing out entirely

If the conflict is confusing or you want to start over:

```bash showLineNumbers
git merge --abort      # cancel an in-progress merge, return to pre-merge state
git rebase --abort     # cancel an in-progress rebase, return to pre-rebase state
```

Both are completely safe — they simply undo the in-progress operation with no side effects.

## Reducing how often conflicts happen

* **Pull/rebase `main` into your branch frequently** — small, frequent conflicts are far easier to resolve than one giant conflict after a two-week-old branch finally merges.
* **Keep branches short-lived and focused** — the less two branches touch the same files, the fewer conflicts.
* **Communicate** — if you and a teammate are both about to touch the same file/function, a 30-second Slack message avoids a conflict entirely.

## Tooling tips

Most editors (VS Code, GoLand) show conflict markers with inline **"Accept Current" / "Accept Incoming" / "Accept Both"** buttons — usually faster and safer than resolving by hand in a plain text editor. `git mergetool` can also launch a configured 3-way diff tool.

title: Undoing Changes
description: reset, revert, restore, and stash — Git's four different ways to undo something, and when to use each.
content:
Git has several "undo" commands that look similar but do very different things. Picking the wrong one is how people lose work — this page is the map.

## Quick decision table

| I want to... | Command |
|---|---|
| Discard uncommitted changes to a file | `git restore <file>` |
| Unstage a file (keep the edits) | `git restore --staged <file>` |
| Temporarily shelve uncommitted work | `git stash` |
| Undo the last commit, but keep the changes | `git reset --soft HEAD~1` |
| Completely delete the last commit and its changes | `git reset --hard HEAD~1` |
| Undo a commit that's already pushed/shared | `git revert <commit>` |

## `git restore` — working directory changes

```bash showLineNumbers
git restore file.go              # discard uncommitted edits to file.go, back to last commit
git restore --staged file.go      # unstage file.go (git add undone), but keep the edits
```

## `git stash` — shelve work temporarily

Useful when you need to switch branches but aren't ready to commit:

```bash showLineNumbers
git stash                 # shelve all uncommitted changes
git stash list             # see stashed entries
git stash pop               # re-apply the most recent stash, and remove it from the stash list
git stash apply             # re-apply the most recent stash, but keep it in the list too
git stash drop               # delete a stash without applying it
```

## `git reset` — move the branch pointer

`reset` moves your current branch's pointer to a different commit. It has three modes, differing in what happens to your working directory and staging area:

```bash showLineNumbers
git reset --soft HEAD~1   # move pointer back 1 commit; keep changes staged
git reset --mixed HEAD~1  # (default) move pointer back; keep changes, but unstaged
git reset --hard HEAD~1   # move pointer back; DELETE all changes, working dir matches that commit
```

<Note title="Danger" type="danger">
  `git reset --hard` permanently discards commits AND uncommitted changes. If those commits have
  already been pushed, resetting locally does not remove them from the remote — you'd need a force
  push, which brings its own risks (see [Working with Remotes](/docs/git-workflow/remotes)).
</Note>

## `git revert` — the safe undo for shared history

Instead of removing a commit, `revert` creates a **new commit** that applies the exact opposite change:

```bash showLineNumbers
git revert a1b2c3d
```

```text showLineNumbers
Before: A - B - C (bad commit) - D
After:  A - B - C - D - C' (reverts C)
```

Because it adds to history rather than rewriting it, `revert` is always safe to use on shared branches like `main` — nobody's local history breaks.

## Which one should you actually use?

title: Git Workflow Strategies
description: Feature Branch Workflow, Git Flow, and Trunk-Based Development compared — and which to pick for a small team.
content:
Everything so far (branching, merging, rebasing) are *mechanics*. A **workflow strategy** is the *policy* a team agrees on for how those mechanics get used — when to branch, how long a branch lives, and how code reaches production.

## Feature Branch Workflow

The simplest and most common strategy: every change (feature, fix, chore) gets its own branch off `main`, and merges back via a pull request once reviewed.

* **Pros:** simple, easy to explain, works with any hosting platform's PR review flow.
* **Cons:** on its own, says nothing about *releases* — fine for a website deployed continuously, less clear for versioned software with scheduled releases.

## Git Flow

A heavier model with dedicated long-lived branches for different purposes:

* `main` — always reflects the latest **released** production code.
* `develop` — integration branch where features land before a release.
* `feature/*` — branched from `develop`, merged back into `develop`.
* `release/*` — branched from `develop` when preparing a release (final testing/bugfixes).
* `hotfix/*` — branched from `main` for urgent production fixes, merged into both `main` and `develop`.

- **Pros:** very explicit about what's released vs in-progress; good for software with scheduled, versioned releases (e.g. mobile apps, installed software).
- **Cons:** heavy process overhead for teams that deploy continuously; overkill for small teams or single-developer projects.

## Trunk-Based Development

The opposite extreme: everyone commits directly to `main` (the "trunk"), or uses very short-lived branches (hours, not weeks) that merge back constantly. Feature flags hide incomplete work in production rather than isolating it in a branch.

* **Pros:** avoids large, painful merges entirely; pairs naturally with continuous deployment and CI/CD.
* **Cons:** requires strong test coverage and CI discipline — without it, `main` breaks often.

## Comparison

| | Feature Branch | Git Flow | Trunk-Based |
|---|---|---|---|
| Branch lifetime | Days | Days–weeks | Hours |
| Best for | Most small/medium teams | Versioned releases (mobile, packaged software) | Continuous deployment, high test coverage |
| Complexity | Low | High | Low (but requires discipline/CI) |
| Release model | Deploy `main` whenever ready | Scheduled releases via `release/*` | Deploy `main` continuously |

## Recommendation for a small or solo project

title: Arrays, Slices & Maps
description: Go's built-in collections, how slices actually work under the hood, and the aliasing gotcha everyone hits.
content:
## Arrays — fixed size, rarely used directly

An array's length is part of its type: `[3]int` and `[4]int` are different types. Arrays are **values** — assigning one copies it.

```go showLineNumbers
var a [3]int          // [0 0 0]
b := [3]string{"x", "y", "z"}
c := [...]int{1, 2, 3} // compiler counts the elements

d := b     // full copy, not a reference
d[0] = "changed"
fmt.Println(b[0]) // still "x"
```

You'll rarely declare arrays directly. They exist mainly as the storage that slices point at.

## Slices — what you'll actually use

A slice is a dynamically-sized view into an array. Under the hood it's a small struct with three fields:

* **ptr** — where the slice starts in the backing array
* **len** — how many elements it currently contains (`len(s)`)
* **cap** — how many it can hold before needing to grow (`cap(s)`)

```go showLineNumbers
var s []int              // nil slice — len 0, cap 0, but usable
s = append(s, 1)

t := []int{1, 2, 3}      // literal
u := make([]int, 0, 10)  // len 0, cap 10 — preallocated
v := make([]int, 5)      // len 5, cap 5 — [0 0 0 0 0]
```

### append and growth

`append` returns a **new slice header** — you must assign the result:

```go showLineNumbers
s = append(s, 4)            // always reassign
s = append(s, 5, 6, 7)      // multiple values
s = append(s, other...)     // append another slice
```

When `len` would exceed `cap`, Go allocates a bigger backing array (roughly doubling) and copies everything over. That's why preallocating matters in hot paths:

```go showLineNumbers
// Good: one allocation instead of repeated grow-and-copy
results := make([]User, 0, len(rows))
for _, row := range rows {
    results = append(results, toUser(row))
}
```

### Slicing

```go showLineNumbers
s := []int{0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5}

s[1:4]   // [1 2 3]  — from index 1 up to (not including) 4
s[:3]    // [0 1 2]
s[2:]    // [2 3 4 5]
s[:]     // whole slice
```

This also matters for function arguments: passing a slice copies the *header*, not the data — so the function can modify your elements, but appending inside it won't be visible to the caller.

## Maps

An unordered key–value store. Keys must be comparable (no slices, maps, or functions as keys).

```go showLineNumbers
// Always create with make or a literal — a nil map panics on write
m := make(map[string]int)
n := map[string]int{"alice": 30, "bob": 25}

m["alice"] = 30          // set
age := m["alice"]        // get
delete(m, "alice")       // delete
count := len(m)          // size
```

### Missing keys and the comma-ok idiom

Reading a missing key returns the value type's **zero value**, not an error — so you can't tell "missing" from "present but zero" without the second return value:

```go showLineNumbers
age := m["nobody"]          // 0 — but does the key exist?

age, ok := m["nobody"]
if !ok {
    // definitely not present
}
```

### Iteration order is random

```go showLineNumbers
for key, value := range m {
    // Order differs on EVERY run — this is deliberate, to stop
    // anyone depending on it.
}

// If you need deterministic order, sort the keys:
keys := make([]string, 0, len(m))
for k := range m {
    keys = append(keys, k)
}
sort.Strings(keys)
for _, k := range keys {
    fmt.Println(k, m[k])
}
```

### Sets

Go has no set type. The idiom is a map with an empty-struct value, which uses zero bytes:

```go showLineNumbers
seen := make(map[string]struct{})
seen["alice"] = struct{}{}

if _, ok := seen["alice"]; ok {
    // present
}
```

## Best practices

* **Preallocate with `make([]T, 0, n)`** when you know roughly how many elements you'll add.
* **Always reassign the result of `append`.**
* **Copy explicitly** when a slice must not share memory with its source — especially before storing it somewhere long-lived.
* **Return empty slices, not nil,** from functions when the caller will marshal to JSON (`nil` encodes as `null`, empty encodes as `[]`). Otherwise `nil` is fine and idiomatic.
* **Use the comma-ok idiom** whenever "missing" and "zero" mean different things.
* **Never rely on map iteration order.** Sort the keys when order matters.

## Why Go for backend work

Go was built at Google to solve a specific problem: large codebases with many engineers were becoming slow to compile and hard to keep consistent. The design choices follow from that:

* **Compiles to a single static binary.** No runtime, no interpreter, no dependency hell on the server. Deploying is copying one file — which is also why Go containers can be tiny.
* **Fast compilation.** Builds take seconds, so the edit → run loop stays tight.
* **Concurrency built into the language.** Goroutines and channels make handling thousands of simultaneous requests natural (covered later in [Concurrency](/docs/concurrency)).
* **Deliberately small.** No inheritance, no generics until recently, one loop keyword. Less to argue about in code review.
* **One official formatter.** `gofmt` ends all formatting debates — every Go codebase looks the same.

The trade-off is verbosity: Go makes you write out error handling explicitly and avoids clever abstractions. That feels tedious at first and pays off when you're reading unfamiliar code at 2am.

## Your first program

Every Go project starts by initializing a module. The module path is normally the repository URL — it's how other code imports your packages.

## The toolchain

These ship with Go — no extra tools to install:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `go run .` | Compile and run in one step. Used constantly during development. |
| `go build` | Compile to a binary in the current directory. |
| `go build -o bin/app ./cmd/api` | Compile a specific package to a named output path. |
| `go test ./...` | Run all tests in the module (`./...` means "this package and everything below"). |
| `go fmt ./...` | Reformat code to the canonical style. |
| `go vet ./...` | Report suspicious constructs the compiler allows but are probably bugs. |
| `go mod tidy` | Add missing dependencies and drop unused ones from `go.mod`. |
| `go get example.com/pkg` | Add or upgrade a dependency. |

## Cross-compiling

One of Go's most useful production tricks — build a Linux binary from your Mac:

```bash showLineNumbers
GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go build -o bin/app ./cmd/api
```

## Best practices

* **Run `go fmt` on save.** Configure your editor to do it automatically — never hand-format Go.
* **Run `go vet ./...` before committing.** It catches real bugs (bad `printf` verbs, unreachable code, lock copying) that compile fine.
* **Use the repo URL as your module path,** even for private projects. Changing it later means updating every import.
* **Commit `go.mod` and `go.sum`.** `go.sum` contains checksums that guarantee everyone builds the exact same dependency code.
* **Run `go mod tidy` after adding or removing imports** to keep dependencies honest.

title: Packages & Modules
description: How Go code is organized into packages and modules — go.mod, imports, exported names, and internal/.
content:
Go has two levels of organization: **packages** (a directory of `.go` files, the unit of compilation and visibility) and **modules** (a collection of packages versioned together, the unit of dependency management).

## Packages

Every `.go` file starts with a package declaration. All files in one directory must declare the same package name:

```go showLineNumbers
package user
```

Conventions:

* **Package name = directory name.** A directory `internal/user/` contains `package user`.
* **Short, lowercase, singular, no underscores:** `user`, `httputil`, `auth` — not `Users`, `user_service`, or `userUtils`.
* **`package main` marks an executable.** It needs a `func main()` and produces a binary; every other package is a library.

### Names are the API — capitalization is the access control

Go has no `public`/`private` keywords. **A capitalized identifier is exported** (visible to other packages); a lowercase one is not:

```go showLineNumbers title="internal/user/user.go"
package user

type User struct {      // exported
    ID   string         // exported field
    Name string         // exported field
    salt string         // unexported — invisible outside this package
}

func New(name string) *User { }   // exported
func hashPassword(s string) { }   // unexported — internal helper
```

## Imports

```go showLineNumbers
import (
    "fmt"           // standard library
    "net/http"

    "github.com/google/uuid"          // third-party

    "github.com/you/app/internal/user" // your own module
)
```

`gofmt`/`goimports` groups and sorts these automatically — standard library first, then everything else. Let the tool do it.

```go showLineNumbers
import (
    "fmt"
    f "fmt"            // alias, for name collisions
    _ "github.com/lib/pq"  // blank import — runs init() only, common for DB drivers
)
```

The import path is the **module path plus the directory**, not the package name — which is why the module path in `go.mod` matters.

## Modules

A module is defined by `go.mod` at the repository root:

```go showLineNumbers title="go.mod"
module github.com/you/app

go 1.25

require (
    github.com/google/uuid v1.6.0
    github.com/jackc/pgx/v5 v5.7.1
)

require (
    golang.org/x/text v0.19.0 // indirect
)
```

* **`module`** — the import path prefix for every package in this repo.
* **`go`** — the language version, which also gates behavior changes (like the Go 1.22 loop variable fix).
* **`require`** — direct dependencies; `// indirect` marks dependencies of your dependencies.

### go.sum

`go.sum` records a cryptographic checksum for every dependency version. If a published module's contents ever change, the build fails instead of silently pulling different code.

### Everyday module commands

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `go mod init github.com/you/app` | Create a new module |
| `go get github.com/pkg/name` | Add or upgrade a dependency |
| `go get -u ./...` | Upgrade all dependencies to latest minor/patch |
| `go mod tidy` | Add anything imported but missing, remove anything unused |
| `go mod download` | Download deps without building (useful for Docker layer caching) |
| `go mod why github.com/pkg/name` | Explain why a dependency is in your graph |

Run `go mod tidy` before committing — it's the module equivalent of cleaning up unused imports.

## internal/ — enforced privacy

A package under a directory named `internal/` can only be imported by code rooted in the parent of that `internal/` directory. The **compiler** enforces this:

Here `internal/user` is importable from anywhere inside `github.com/you/app`, but **no other module can import it** — even though it's a public GitHub repo. `pkg/httputil` is importable by anyone.

## init()

A package may define `func init()`, which runs once before `main()`. Use it rarely — it runs implicitly, which makes program startup hard to follow and hard to test.

```go showLineNumbers
func init() {
    // Prefer explicit setup in main() over this.
}
```

## Best practices

* **Name packages for what they provide,** not what they contain. Avoid grab-bag packages named `util`, `common`, `helpers`, or `models` — they attract unrelated code forever.
* **Keep the exported surface small.** Export only what callers need; everything else stays lowercase.
* **Use `internal/`** for application code by default.
* **Use the repo URL as the module path** from day one.
* **Run `go mod tidy` before committing.**
* **Avoid circular imports** — Go forbids them outright. If two packages need each other, the shared piece usually wants to be a third package (or an interface defined in the consumer).

Project layout at a larger scale — where handlers, services, and repositories live — is covered in [Code Organization](/docs/code-organization).

title: Pointers
description: What pointers are in Go, why they exist without pointer arithmetic, and when you actually need one.
content:
## Everything in Go is passed by value

This is the single most important thing to understand. When you pass something to a function, Go copies it. Always.

```go showLineNumbers
func increment(n int) {
    n++   // modifies the copy
}

count := 5
increment(count)
fmt.Println(count) // still 5
```

A pointer is how you opt out: instead of passing the value, you pass its **memory address**, so the function can reach the original.

## Syntax

Two operators, and they're mirror images:

* `&x` — "address of x", gives you a pointer
* `*p` — "value at p", dereferences the pointer

```go showLineNumbers
count := 5
p := &count        // p is of type *int

fmt.Println(p)     // 0xc000018030 — an address
fmt.Println(*p)    // 5 — the value it points to

*p = 10            // write through the pointer
fmt.Println(count) // 10 — the original changed
```

Now the function version works:

```go showLineNumbers
func increment(n *int) {
    *n++
}

count := 5
increment(&count)
fmt.Println(count) // 6
```

## The zero value is nil

```go showLineNumbers
var p *int          // nil
fmt.Println(p == nil) // true

fmt.Println(*p)     // PANIC: runtime error: invalid memory address
```

Dereferencing a nil pointer crashes your program. This is the most common runtime panic in Go, and it usually comes from an unchecked error:

```go showLineNumbers
user, err := findUser(id)
// forgetting to check err here...
fmt.Println(user.Name)  // panics if findUser returned (nil, err)
```

## Pointers to structs

Go automatically dereferences struct pointers on field access, so you almost never write `(*u).Name`:

```go showLineNumbers
type User struct {
    Name string
    Age  int
}

u := &User{Name: "alice", Age: 30}

fmt.Println(u.Name)     // Go does this for you
fmt.Println((*u).Name)  // equivalent, but nobody writes this

u.Age = 31              // modifies the original
```

## new vs \&T{}

```go showLineNumbers
p := new(int)        // pointer to a zero-valued int
u := &User{}         // pointer to a zero-valued User — preferred
u2 := &User{Name: "bob"}  // with field values
```

`new` is rarely used in practice. Use `&T{...}` — it's more flexible and reads better.

## No pointer arithmetic

Unlike C, you cannot do `p++` to walk through memory. Go deliberately removed this: it's the source of most memory-safety bugs, and slices already cover the legitimate use case. Combined with garbage collection, this means Go pointers are safe — you can't create a dangling pointer or read past the end of an allocation.

## When should you use a pointer?

| Use a pointer when... | Use a value when... |
|---|---|
| The function must modify the caller's data | The data is read-only in the function |
| The struct is large and copying is expensive | The struct is small (a few fields) |
| `nil` is a meaningful state ("not found", "not set") | There's always a valid value |
| The type has pointer-receiver methods (mutex, etc.) | The type is a simple value type |

```go showLineNumbers
// Pointer: needs to modify, and nil means "not found"
func FindUser(id string) (*User, error)

// Value: small, read-only
func FormatName(u User) string

// Pointer: contains a sync.Mutex, must never be copied
type Server struct {
    mu sync.Mutex
    // ...
}
func NewServer() *Server
```

## Best practices

* **Don't reach for pointers by default.** Values are simpler, safe to share across goroutines, and often faster for small structs.
* **Check every error before dereferencing** the value returned alongside it.
* **Be consistent within a type** — if any method needs a pointer receiver, use pointer receivers for all of them (covered in [Structs & Methods](/docs/golang-fundamentals/structs-methods)).
* **Never copy a struct containing a `sync.Mutex`.** Always pass it as a pointer; `go vet` catches this.
* **Use `nil` deliberately** as "absent", and document it — a `*string` field in a struct is a reasonable way to distinguish "empty string" from "not provided" when parsing JSON.

title: Variables, Types & Constants
description: Declaring variables, Go's zero values, type conversion, and constants with iota.
content:
## Declaring variables

Go has two forms. Inside a function, the short form is idiomatic:

```go showLineNumbers
// Short declaration — type inferred. Only valid inside functions.
name := "alice"
count := 42

// Full form — required at package level, or when you want an explicit type
// or the zero value.
var name string = "alice"
var count int
var ready bool
```

Use `:=` by default. Reach for `var` when you specifically want the zero value (`var buf bytes.Buffer`) or when declaring at package scope.

## Zero values

Every type has a zero value, and variables are **never** uninitialized garbage. This is a real safety feature — there's no "undefined" in Go.

| Type | Zero value |
|---|---|
| `int`, `int64`, `float64` | `0` |
| `string` | `""` (empty, not `nil`) |
| `bool` | `false` |
| Pointers, slices, maps, channels, functions, interfaces | `nil` |
| `struct` | A struct with every field set to its own zero value |

```go showLineNumbers
var count int      // 0
var name string    // ""
var items []string // nil — but you can still call len() and append() on it

fmt.Println(len(items)) // 0, no panic
items = append(items, "first") // works fine on a nil slice
```

## Basic types

```go showLineNumbers
// Integers — int is 64-bit on modern platforms. Use int unless you have a
// specific reason (binary formats, memory pressure, matching an API).
var i int
var i8 int8; var i64 int64
var u uint; var u8 uint8   // byte is an alias for uint8

// Floats — use float64 unless you have a reason not to.
var f float64

// Strings are immutable UTF-8 byte sequences.
var s string

// rune is an alias for int32 and represents one Unicode code point.
var r rune = 'A'
```

## Type conversion is always explicit

Go never converts between numeric types automatically. This is verbose but eliminates a whole class of silent precision bugs.

```go showLineNumbers
var i int = 42
var f float64 = float64(i)   // required — `var f float64 = i` will not compile
var u uint = uint(f)

// Same for strings and byte slices:
b := []byte("hello")
s := string(b)
```

## Constants

Constants are computed at compile time and can be untyped, which lets them adapt to context:

```go showLineNumbers
const MaxRetries = 3
const AppName = "payments-api"

// Untyped constants take on the type they're used with:
const timeout = 30
var d time.Duration = timeout * time.Second  // works — timeout adapts

// Grouped:
const (
    StatusActive   = "active"
    StatusInactive = "inactive"
)
```

## iota — enumerations

`iota` is a counter that resets to 0 in each `const` block and increments per line. It's how Go does enums:

```go showLineNumbers
type Status int

const (
    StatusPending Status = iota // 0
    StatusActive                // 1
    StatusSuspended             // 2
    StatusClosed                // 3
)

// Give it a String() method so it prints readably instead of as a number:
func (s Status) String() string {
    switch s {
    case StatusPending:
        return "pending"
    case StatusActive:
        return "active"
    case StatusSuspended:
        return "suspended"
    case StatusClosed:
        return "closed"
    default:
        return "unknown"
    }
}
```

Defining `type Status int` rather than using a bare `int` means the compiler stops you passing an arbitrary number where a `Status` is expected — cheap type safety.

## Best practices

* **Prefer `:=` inside functions**, `var` for zero values and package-level declarations.
* **Use `int` for counts and indexes** unless a specific size is required.
* **Use `float64`, not `float32`,** unless you're matching an external format.
* **Never use floats for money.** Use integer minor units (cents) or a decimal library — floating point cannot represent `0.1` exactly.
* **Name constants and group related ones** in a single `const` block with a defined type.
* **Keep names short in small scopes.** `i`, `err`, `w`, `r` are idiomatic Go, not laziness. Longer names belong to package-level identifiers.

title: Aggregation & Grouping
description: COUNT, SUM, AVG, GROUP BY, and HAVING — computing summaries in the database instead of in application code.
content:
## Aggregate functions

An aggregate collapses many rows into a single value:

```sql showLineNumbers
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders;
SELECT SUM(quantity) FROM orders;
SELECT AVG(price_cents) FROM products;
SELECT MIN(created_at), MAX(created_at) FROM orders;
```

| Function | Returns |
|---|---|
| `COUNT(*)` | Number of rows |
| `COUNT(col)` | Number of rows where `col` is **not null** |
| `COUNT(DISTINCT col)` | Number of distinct non-null values |
| `SUM(col)` | Total |
| `AVG(col)` | Mean |
| `MIN` / `MAX` | Smallest / largest |

Aggregates ignore `NULL` generally, which also affects `AVG`:

```sql showLineNumbers
-- AVG divides by the count of NON-NULL values, not the row count.
-- If you want nulls treated as zero, be explicit:
SELECT AVG(COALESCE(score, 0)) FROM reviews;
```

## GROUP BY

`GROUP BY` splits rows into groups and applies the aggregate to each group separately:

```sql showLineNumbers
-- One row per status, with the count for each
SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY status;
```

| status | order\_count |
|---|---|
| pending | 12 |
| paid | 45 |
| shipped | 30 |

### The GROUP BY rule

Every column in `SELECT` must either be **in the `GROUP BY`** or **wrapped in an aggregate**. PostgreSQL enforces this strictly:

```sql showLineNumbers
-- Error: column "o.id" must appear in the GROUP BY clause
-- or be used in an aggregate function
SELECT status, id, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY status;

-- Fine
SELECT status, COUNT(*), MAX(id) FROM orders GROUP BY status;
```

The reason is simple: if 45 rows share a status, which single `id` would the database show you? Either pick one with an aggregate (`MAX(id)`) or group by it too.

### Grouping by multiple columns

```sql showLineNumbers
SELECT user_id, status, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM orders
GROUP BY user_id, status
ORDER BY user_id, status;
```

One row per distinct combination.

### Grouping with joins

The common real-world shape — a summary per user:

```sql showLineNumbers
SELECT u.id, u.name, COUNT(o.id) AS order_count, SUM(o.quantity) AS total_items
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
GROUP BY u.id, u.name
ORDER BY order_count DESC;
```

## HAVING

`WHERE` filters rows *before* grouping; `HAVING` filters groups *after*. Aggregates can only be used in `HAVING`:

```sql showLineNumbers
-- Users with more than 5 orders
SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY user_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;

-- Error: aggregates are not allowed in WHERE
SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE COUNT(*) > 5 GROUP BY user_id;
```

Both together — filter rows first, then filter the resulting groups:

```sql showLineNumbers
SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS paid_orders, SUM(quantity) AS items
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'              -- discard non-paid rows first
GROUP BY user_id
HAVING SUM(quantity) > 10          -- then keep only big-volume users
ORDER BY items DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

## Aggregate with FILTER

A PostgreSQL feature that's cleaner than the `CASE WHEN` trick for conditional counts:

```sql showLineNumbers
SELECT
    COUNT(*) AS total,
    COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid')      AS paid,
    COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'cancelled') AS cancelled
FROM orders;
```

One pass over the table, several different counts.

## Best practices

title: Constraints & Keys
description: Primary keys, foreign keys, and constraints — letting the database enforce correctness instead of your application.
content:
## Why constraints matter

Constraints are rules the database enforces on every write, no matter where it came from. That's the key point: your Go service might validate input carefully, but a migration script, an admin running SQL by hand, a background job, or a second service can all write to the same table. A constraint is the one check none of them can skip.

## NOT NULL

```sql showLineNumbers
name TEXT NOT NULL,
```

Rejects rows where the column is missing. Default to `NOT NULL` and only allow nulls where "unknown" or "not applicable" is a real, meaningful state — because every nullable column complicates every query that reads it (see [NULL handling](/docs/sql-postgresql-basics/querying#working-with-null)).

## UNIQUE

```sql showLineNumbers
email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,

-- Multi-column: the combination must be unique, not each column separately
CONSTRAINT one_review_per_user UNIQUE (user_id, product_id)
```

## CHECK

Enforce any boolean condition on a row:

```sql showLineNumbers
price_cents INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (price_cents >= 0),
quantity    INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
status      TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('pending', 'paid', 'shipped', 'cancelled')),

-- Named, and referencing multiple columns
CONSTRAINT valid_date_range CHECK (ends_at > starts_at)
```

Cheap to add and they catch entire categories of bugs — a negative price simply cannot exist in the table.

## Primary keys

The column that uniquely identifies a row. Implies `NOT NULL` + `UNIQUE`, and PostgreSQL creates an index for it automatically:

```sql showLineNumbers
id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,

-- Composite: for join tables, where the pair is the identity
CREATE TABLE order_tags (
    order_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id),
    tag_id   BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES tags(id),
    PRIMARY KEY (order_id, tag_id)
);
```

Every table should have one. Without it, you have no reliable way to reference or update a specific row.

## Foreign keys

A foreign key says "this column must contain a value that exists in that other table." This is **referential integrity** — the guarantee that an order can never point at a user who doesn't exist.

```sql showLineNumbers
CREATE TABLE orders (
    id         BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id    BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
    product_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id),
    quantity   INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1 CHECK (quantity > 0)
);
```

Now these both fail, which is exactly what you want:

```sql showLineNumbers
-- Fails: user 999 doesn't exist
INSERT INTO orders (user_id, product_id) VALUES (999, 1);

-- Fails: user 1 still has orders referencing them
DELETE FROM users WHERE id = 1;
```

### ON DELETE behavior

You control what happens when the referenced row is deleted:

```sql showLineNumbers
-- Default: block the delete while children exist. Safest.
user_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,

-- Delete the children too. Powerful and dangerous.
user_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,

-- Keep the child row, null out the reference (column must be nullable)
user_id BIGINT REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
```

| Option | Deleting a user... |
|---|---|
| `RESTRICT` (default) | Fails if they have orders |
| `CASCADE` | Deletes all their orders too |
| `SET NULL` | Keeps orders, sets `user_id` to `NULL` |

<Note title="Foreign keys are not indexed automatically" type="warning">
  PostgreSQL indexes the primary key side, but **not** the referencing column. `orders.user_id`
  has no index unless you create one — and without it, both `WHERE user_id = ?` lookups and
  cascading deletes do a full table scan. Add it:

  ```sql
  CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_id ON orders(user_id);
  ```

  This is one of the most common causes of slow queries in a young codebase. See
  [Indexes](/docs/sql-postgresql-basics/indexes).
</Note>

## Adding constraints later

```sql showLineNumbers
ALTER TABLE users ADD CONSTRAINT users_email_unique UNIQUE (email);
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_qty_positive CHECK (quantity > 0);
ALTER TABLE orders
    ADD CONSTRAINT orders_user_fk FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id);

ALTER TABLE orders DROP CONSTRAINT orders_qty_positive;
```

Adding a constraint fails if existing rows violate it — which is useful information, but means you must clean up the data first.

## Best practices

* **Every table gets a primary key.**
* **Every reference between tables gets a foreign key.** The small write cost buys you a guarantee that your data is never structurally broken.
* **Index your foreign key columns.**
* **Default to `NOT NULL`;** allow nulls deliberately.
* **Name your constraints** (`orders_qty_positive`) rather than letting PostgreSQL generate names — error messages become readable and dropping them later is straightforward.
* **Add `CHECK` constraints liberally.** They're nearly free and document your assumptions in the schema itself.
* **Handle constraint violations as expected errors** in application code, rather than trying to pre-check for them.

title: Indexes: The Basics
description: What a database index actually is, when to add one, what it costs, and how to check whether it's being used.
content:
## What an index is

Without an index, finding `WHERE email = 'alice@example.com'` means reading **every row** in the table — a *sequential scan*. That's fine for 100 rows and unusable for 10 million.

An index is a separate, sorted data structure that lets PostgreSQL jump straight to matching rows, much like the index at the back of a book. The default type is a **B-tree**, which suits equality and range comparisons.

## Creating indexes

```sql showLineNumbers
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_id ON orders(user_id);

-- Composite: one index covering several columns
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_status ON orders(user_id, status);

-- Unique index — also enforces uniqueness, like a UNIQUE constraint
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);

-- Partial: index only some rows, keeping it small
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_pending ON orders(created_at) WHERE status = 'pending';

DROP INDEX idx_orders_user_id;
```

## What already has an index

PostgreSQL creates indexes automatically for:

* **`PRIMARY KEY`** columns
* **`UNIQUE`** constraints

It does **not** create one for foreign key columns:

```sql showLineNumbers
-- orders.user_id REFERENCES users(id) has NO index by default
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_id ON orders(user_id);
```

## When to add an index

Index a column when it appears in:

* **`WHERE` clauses** you run often
* **`JOIN` conditions** (i.e. foreign keys)
* **`ORDER BY`** on large tables — a matching index avoids a sort
* **`UNIQUE` constraints** (automatic)

## What indexes cost

Indexes aren't free, which is why "index everything" is the wrong strategy:

* **Writes get slower.** Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` must update every affected index. A table with 8 indexes has substantially slower writes than one with 2.
* **They consume disk and memory.** An index on a large table can be gigabytes, competing for cache space with your actual data.
* **They need maintenance.** More indexes mean more vacuum work.

## Composite index column order matters

A composite index works **left to right**. `(user_id, status)` can serve:

```sql showLineNumbers
WHERE user_id = 1                      -- yes, uses the index
WHERE user_id = 1 AND status = 'paid'  -- yes, uses both columns
WHERE status = 'paid'                  -- NO — status is not the leading column
```

Put the column used for **equality** first, and the more selective column first when both are equality checks. A separate index on `status` alone would be needed for that last query.

## Checking whether an index is used

`EXPLAIN` shows the plan; `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` actually runs the query and reports real timings:

```sql showLineNumbers
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42;
```

```text showLineNumbers
Index Scan using idx_orders_user_id on orders  (cost=0.29..8.31 rows=1 width=48)
                                               (actual time=0.021..0.023 rows=3 loops=1)
  Index Cond: (user_id = 42)
Planning Time: 0.083 ms
Execution Time: 0.041 ms
```

What to look for:

| Plan node | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Index Scan` | Using an index — good |
| `Index Only Scan` | Answered entirely from the index, no table access — best |
| `Bitmap Heap Scan` | Index used for many matching rows — usually fine |
| `Seq Scan` | Reading the whole table — fine on small tables, a red flag on large ones |

## Finding unused indexes

```sql showLineNumbers
SELECT relname AS table, indexrelname AS index, idx_scan AS times_used
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes
WHERE idx_scan = 0
ORDER BY relname;
```

Indexes with `idx_scan = 0` have never been used since statistics were last reset — candidates for removal (excluding those backing constraints).

## Best practices

* **Index every foreign key column.**
* **Add indexes for measured slow queries**, not speculatively.
* **Use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`** on production tables.
* **Mind composite column order** — leftmost columns are what count.
* **Name indexes consistently**, e.g. `idx_<table>_<columns>`.
* **Verify with `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`** on realistic data volumes — an index that isn't used is worse than no index.
* **Review and drop unused indexes** periodically.

Query plans in depth, index types beyond B-tree (GIN, GiST, BRIN), and diagnosing N+1 queries are covered in [Query Optimization](/docs/query-optimization).

title: Introduction & Setup
description: What relational databases are, why PostgreSQL, and getting a server running locally with Docker and psql.
content:
## What a relational database is

A relational database stores data in **tables** — rows and columns, like a spreadsheet with rules. The "relational" part is that tables reference each other: an order row points at the user who placed it, rather than duplicating that user's details.

Two things make this worth using over files or a key–value store:

* **The database enforces correctness.** Types, required fields, uniqueness, and references between tables are all checked by the database itself. Bad data gets rejected regardless of which service or script tried to write it.
* **You describe *what* you want, not *how* to get it.** SQL is declarative. You write "give me these rows joined with those, sorted by date"; the query planner figures out the fastest way to do it.

## Why PostgreSQL

It's the default choice for most backend teams:

* **Open source**, no licensing cost, no vendor lock-in.
* **Strict about correctness** — it won't silently truncate your data or coerce a bad value the way some databases will.
* **Full ACID transactions** (covered in [Transactions](/docs/sql-postgresql-basics/transactions)).
* **Far more than a plain table store** — JSONB, full-text search, geospatial data, and array columns are all built in, so you often don't need a second datastore.

## Running PostgreSQL locally

Docker is the fastest way, and it keeps your machine clean:

<Note title="Named volumes matter" type="warning">
  The plain `docker run` above stores data inside the container — remove the container and your
  data is gone. That's fine for scratch work, but use the Compose version with a named volume
  (`pgdata`) for anything you want to keep between restarts.
</Note>

## Connecting with psql

`psql` is PostgreSQL's interactive terminal. Learning a handful of its commands saves a lot of time:

```bash showLineNumbers
# Connect (into the Docker container)
docker exec -it pg psql -U postgres -d shop

# Or from your machine, using a connection URL
psql "postgres://postgres:secret@localhost:5432/shop"
```

Once connected, backslash commands inspect the database:

| Command | What it shows |
|---|---|
| `\l` | List all databases |
| `\c dbname` | Connect to a different database |
| `\dt` | List tables |
| `\d users` | Describe the `users` table — columns, types, indexes, constraints |
| `\di` | List indexes |
| `\x` | Toggle expanded output (great for wide rows) |
| `\timing` | Show how long each query takes |
| `\?` | Help for backslash commands |
| `\q` | Quit |

## The schema used throughout this section

Every page from here uses this small e-commerce schema, so examples build on each other:

```sql showLineNumbers title="schema.sql"
CREATE TABLE users (
    id         BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    email      TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    name       TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE products (
    id    BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name  TEXT NOT NULL,
    price_cents INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (price_cents >= 0)
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
    id         BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id    BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
    product_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id),
    quantity   INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
```

title: Joins
description: Combining rows across tables with INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL joins — plus the mistakes that produce wrong results.
content:
## What a join does

A join combines rows from two tables based on a condition — usually matching a foreign key to a primary key. It's how you reassemble the data that normalization split apart.

Using the schema from the [introduction](/docs/sql-postgresql-basics/introduction#the-schema-used-throughout-this-section):

```sql showLineNumbers
SELECT u.name, o.quantity, o.status
FROM orders o
JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.id;
```

`o` and `u` are table aliases — they keep queries readable once more than one table is involved, and they're required when both tables have a column with the same name (like `id`).

## INNER JOIN

Returns only rows where the condition matches on **both** sides. `JOIN` alone means `INNER JOIN`.

```sql showLineNumbers
SELECT u.name, p.name AS product, o.quantity
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.id
INNER JOIN products p ON o.product_id = p.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid';
```

Users with no orders don't appear. Orders with no matching user don't appear (and with a foreign key in place, can't exist).

## LEFT JOIN

Returns **every** row from the left table, plus matching rows from the right. Where there's no match, the right side's columns are `NULL`.

This is what you want for "all X, with their Y if they have any":

```sql showLineNumbers
-- Every user, including those who have never ordered
SELECT u.name, o.id AS order_id
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id;
```

| name | order\_id |
|---|---|
| alice | 1 |
| alice | 2 |
| bob | *NULL* |

### Finding rows with no match

A LEFT JOIN plus `IS NULL` is the standard way to find "records without any related record":

```sql showLineNumbers
-- Users who have never placed an order
SELECT u.id, u.name
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;
```

## RIGHT and FULL

```sql showLineNumbers
-- RIGHT JOIN: all rows from the right table. Rare — just flip the tables
-- and use LEFT JOIN, which is easier to read.
SELECT u.name, o.id FROM users u RIGHT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id;

-- FULL OUTER JOIN: all rows from both sides, NULLs where there's no match.
SELECT u.name, o.id FROM users u FULL JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id;
```

In practice you'll write `INNER` and `LEFT` joins almost exclusively.

## CROSS JOIN

Every row paired with every row — the Cartesian product. Occasionally useful for generating combinations, but usually a symptom of a mistake:

```sql showLineNumbers
SELECT * FROM users CROSS JOIN products;   -- 100 users × 50 products = 5,000 rows
```

## Self joins

A table joined to itself, using two different aliases — for hierarchies and comparisons within one table:

```sql showLineNumbers
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id;
```

## WHERE vs ON in an outer join

This distinction produces genuinely wrong results, and it's worth understanding properly:

```sql showLineNumbers
-- A: condition in ON — filters which rows are joined.
-- Every user still appears; only 'paid' orders get attached.
SELECT u.name, o.id
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id AND o.status = 'paid';

-- B: condition in WHERE — filters AFTER the join.
-- Users with no paid order have o.status = NULL, which fails the test,
-- so they're dropped. This silently behaves like an INNER JOIN.
SELECT u.name, o.id
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid';
```

## Joins and duplicated rows

A join to a one-to-many relationship multiplies rows on the left side:

```sql showLineNumbers
-- If alice has 3 orders, "alice" appears 3 times
SELECT u.name, o.id FROM users u JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id;
```

This is correct behavior, but it means **counting after a join can double-count**:

```sql showLineNumbers
-- Wrong if a user has multiple orders — counts order rows, not users
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users u JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id;

-- Right
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT u.id) FROM users u JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id;
```

## Best practices

* **Always use explicit `JOIN ... ON`,** never the comma-separated form.
* **Alias your tables** with short, meaningful names and qualify every column (`u.id`, not bare `id`).
* **Index the columns you join on** — a foreign key column with no index makes joins slow ([Indexes](/docs/sql-postgresql-basics/indexes)).
* **Put right-table conditions in `ON`** for outer joins.
* **Watch for row multiplication** when joining one-to-many, especially before aggregating.
* **Join only the tables you need.** Every extra join is more work for the planner and more chances to duplicate rows.

description: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, upserts with ON CONFLICT, and PostgreSQL's RETURNING clause.
content:
## INSERT

```sql showLineNumbers
INSERT INTO users (email, name)
VALUES ('alice@example.com', 'Alice');

-- Multiple rows in one statement — much faster than one INSERT per row
INSERT INTO users (email, name) VALUES
    ('bob@example.com', 'Bob'),
    ('carol@example.com', 'Carol');
```

Always list the column names. `INSERT INTO users VALUES (...)` depends on column order and breaks the moment someone adds a column.

Columns you omit get their `DEFAULT` (or `NULL`), which is why `id` and `created_at` don't need to be supplied.

### RETURNING

A PostgreSQL feature worth knowing on day one: get values back from a write without a second query.

```sql showLineNumbers
INSERT INTO users (email, name)
VALUES ('dave@example.com', 'Dave')
RETURNING id, created_at;
```

This is how you obtain a generated `id` — no `SELECT` afterwards, no race condition, one round trip. It works on `UPDATE` and `DELETE` too.

## UPDATE

```sql showLineNumbers
UPDATE users SET name = 'Alice Smith' WHERE id = 1;

-- Multiple columns
UPDATE orders
SET status = 'shipped', updated_at = now()
WHERE id = 42;

-- Computed from the current value
UPDATE orders SET quantity = quantity + 1 WHERE id = 42;
```

### UPDATE from another table

```sql showLineNumbers
UPDATE orders o
SET status = 'cancelled'
FROM users u
WHERE o.user_id = u.id AND u.is_active = false;
```

## DELETE

```sql showLineNumbers
DELETE FROM orders WHERE id = 42;
DELETE FROM orders WHERE status = 'cancelled' AND created_at < now() - INTERVAL '1 year';

DELETE FROM orders;        -- deletes every row. Same warning as UPDATE.
```

`TRUNCATE` empties a table far faster than `DELETE`, but it can't be filtered and is more disruptive:

```sql showLineNumbers
TRUNCATE orders;
TRUNCATE orders RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE;   -- also resets the id sequence
```

Use `TRUNCATE` for resetting test data; use `DELETE` in application code.

### Soft deletes

Often you don't want data to actually disappear — for audit trails, recovery, or referential integrity:

```sql showLineNumbers
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN deleted_at TIMESTAMPTZ;

-- "Delete"
UPDATE users SET deleted_at = now() WHERE id = 1;

-- Every read must then exclude them
SELECT * FROM users WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;
```

## Upsert — INSERT ... ON CONFLICT

"Insert, or update if it already exists." Doing this with a `SELECT` then `INSERT` is a race condition; `ON CONFLICT` is atomic and correct.

```sql showLineNumbers
-- Update the existing row on conflict
INSERT INTO users (email, name)
VALUES ('alice@example.com', 'Alice Updated')
ON CONFLICT (email)
DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name
RETURNING id;

-- Or just ignore the conflict
INSERT INTO users (email, name)
VALUES ('alice@example.com', 'Alice')
ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING;
```

`EXCLUDED` refers to the row you *tried* to insert, so `EXCLUDED.name` is the new value. The conflict target (`email`) must have a `UNIQUE` constraint or index.

## Bulk inserts

Inserting rows one at a time in a loop is the single most common performance mistake with a new database. Each statement is a full network round trip:

```sql showLineNumbers
-- Slow: 1000 round trips
INSERT INTO orders (user_id, product_id) VALUES (1, 1);
INSERT INTO orders (user_id, product_id) VALUES (1, 2);
-- ...

-- Fast: one round trip
INSERT INTO orders (user_id, product_id) VALUES (1, 1), (1, 2), (1, 3);
```

For very large loads (tens of thousands of rows), `COPY` is faster still, and pgx exposes it via `CopyFrom` — see [Using PostgreSQL from Go](/docs/sql-postgresql-basics/using-from-go).

## Best practices

* **Always name your columns in `INSERT`.**
* **Write `WHERE` before `SET`** in an `UPDATE`, and `SELECT` first to confirm the target rows.
* **Use `RETURNING`** to get generated IDs instead of a follow-up query.
* **Use `ON CONFLICT` for upserts,** never check-then-insert.
* **Batch your inserts** rather than looping single-row statements.
* **Wrap multi-statement changes in a transaction** so they succeed or fail together.
* **Add `updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ`** and set it on every update — you'll want it for debugging and syncing.

description: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT, operators, and the NULL rules that surprise everyone.
content:
## SELECT

```sql showLineNumbers
SELECT id, name, email FROM users;

SELECT * FROM users;              -- all columns

SELECT name AS full_name FROM users;   -- rename output column
```

## WHERE

```sql showLineNumbers
SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = 1;
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE quantity > 5;
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status != 'cancelled';

-- Combine with AND / OR, and use parentheses to be explicit
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
  AND (quantity > 10 OR created_at > now() - INTERVAL '7 days');
```

### Comparison operators

| Operator | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `=` `!=` (or `<>`) | Equal, not equal |
| `<` `>` `<=` `>=` | Ordering comparisons |
| `BETWEEN a AND b` | Inclusive range |
| `IN (...)` | Matches any value in a list |
| `LIKE` / `ILIKE` | Pattern match (`ILIKE` is case-insensitive) |
| `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL` | Null check |

```sql showLineNumbers
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE quantity BETWEEN 1 AND 10;
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status IN ('paid', 'shipped');
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email LIKE '%@example.com';
SELECT * FROM users WHERE name ILIKE 'ali%';       -- matches "Alice", "alice"
```

`LIKE` patterns use `%` for "any sequence of characters" and `_` for "exactly one character".

## Working with NULL

`NULL` means "unknown", not "empty" — and that has consequences that catch everyone at least once.

```sql showLineNumbers
-- These NEVER match, even for rows where the column IS null:
SELECT * FROM users WHERE phone = NULL;    -- returns nothing
SELECT * FROM users WHERE phone != NULL;   -- returns nothing

-- Correct:
SELECT * FROM users WHERE phone IS NULL;
SELECT * FROM users WHERE phone IS NOT NULL;
```

Any comparison with `NULL` yields `NULL` (not true, not false), and `WHERE` only keeps rows where the condition is *true*.

`COALESCE` returns the first non-null argument — the standard way to supply a fallback:

```sql showLineNumbers
SELECT name, COALESCE(phone, 'not provided') AS phone FROM users;
```

## ORDER BY

```sql showLineNumbers
SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY created_at DESC;
SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY name ASC;             -- ASC is the default
SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY status, created_at DESC;  -- multiple keys

-- Control where nulls land
SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY phone NULLS LAST;
```

## LIMIT and OFFSET

```sql showLineNumbers
SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY id LIMIT 10;             -- first 10
SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY id LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20;   -- page 3
```

## DISTINCT

```sql showLineNumbers
SELECT DISTINCT status FROM orders;
SELECT DISTINCT user_id, status FROM orders;   -- distinct combinations
```

## Logical order of evaluation

SQL doesn't run in the order you write it. Knowing the real order explains a lot of otherwise confusing errors:

Because `SELECT` runs *after* `WHERE`, an alias defined in `SELECT` can't be used in `WHERE`:

```sql showLineNumbers
-- Error: column "full_name" does not exist
SELECT name AS full_name FROM users WHERE full_name = 'alice';

-- But ORDER BY runs after SELECT, so this works fine:
SELECT name AS full_name FROM users ORDER BY full_name;
```

It also explains why `WHERE` can't filter on aggregates — that's what `HAVING` is for, covered in [Aggregation](/docs/sql-postgresql-basics/aggregation).

## Best practices

* **List columns explicitly** instead of `SELECT *` in application code.
* **Always pair `LIMIT` with `ORDER BY`.**
* **Use `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL`,** never `= NULL`.
* **Prefer `NOT EXISTS` over `NOT IN`** when a subquery might produce nulls.
* **Use keyset pagination** rather than large `OFFSET` values.
* **Format multi-line queries** with keywords starting each line — you'll read these far more often than you write them.
